#79566. Latest Update: An Internal Locus Of Control Makes You A Happier, Wealthier Investor

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1815 w)

Latest Update: An Internal Locus Of Control Makes You A Happier, Wealthier Investor

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an internal locus of control is the belief that you control your outcomes and can solve problems as they come up.
  • Peter Gray, a research psychologist at Boston College argues in his newly introduced book, Restoring Childhood, that kids have become more anxious and depressed over the decades because adults took away their free play and independence.
  • And psychologists have long known that a weak internal locus of control is strongly linked to anxiety and depression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an internal locus of control is the belief that you control your outcomes and can solve problems as they come up. An external locus of control is the belief that outside forces run your life. Luck. The economy. Your boss. Some CEO you’ve never met.

Peter Gray, a research psychologist at Boston College argues in his newly introduced book, Restoring Childhood, that kids have become more anxious and depressed over the decades because adults took away their free play and independence. Children who never get to solve their own problems never build an internal locus of control.

And psychologists have long known that a weak internal locus of control is strongly linked to anxiety and depression.

It makes sense. If you believe you have little control over what happens to you, the world feels cruel. At the extreme, you feel helpless. And when you feel helpless, darker thoughts start creeping in.

As a father of young children, this hit home. As an investor, it hit my wallet. Recently, I got a $50,000 lesson in what it feels like to have zero control.

Recent findings suggest that from an investor’s point of view, the active investor has an internal locus of control. He believes his research and decisions can beat the market.

In a recent development, the passive investor has more of an external locus of control. He accepts that he can’t beat the market, so he buys the whole thing and lets it ride.

In a recent development, the irony is, despite the better feeling of being in control, most active investors underperform over time. I agree with that, which is why about 60% to 70% of my public investments are in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq.

But I have two problems with fully going passive.

According to recent reports, first, I don’t want to earn the same returns as everybody else. I want to outperform so my family’s buying power grows faster than the masses. If not, we'll just be running in place with every other passive index investor.

According to recent reports, second, accepting that I have no control makes me less satisfied. I want to believe my decisions matter. So I keep a chunk of my portfolio in individual stocks. One of them was Nvidia for the past several years.

My Nvidia position was worth about $150,000 in October 2026. It’s now worth about $100,000.

Sources indicate that about $30,000 of the decline came from the broader AI selloff. Fine. That’s the market. I can live with that.

The other $20,000 came from Jensen.

First he admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. U.S. officials reportedly believe she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

It has been revealed that then the Fresh York Times reported a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days later, Jensen resigned as the board moved to oust him. The stock dropped again.

Finding and keeping love truly is harder than getting rich.

In a recent development, losing $50,000 is about a year and a half of food for my family of four. It’s also about a year and a half of the unsubsidized health insurance premiums we pay.

As the household’s provider, I feel like a failure for blowing up so much money. Without a steady day job, our investment returns are what keep us going. Every loss hits harder.

But mostly, I’m annoyed with myself for putting too much capital in one company.

Here’s the uncomfortable part. Blaming Jensen is the external locus of control response.

Sources indicate that an external locus of control means believing outside forces decide your fate. When I say “Jensen cost me $20,000,” I’m pinning my loss on a guy I’ve never met and can’t control.

Sources indicate that it may be true. But it leaves me helpless. I can’t stop the next CEO from falling for someone he shouldn’t. I can’t make a board build a succession plan. And I definitely can’t make billionaires stay faithful.

So the internal locus of control question is: what could I have controlled?

Recent findings suggest that plenty, it turns out. I chose the position size. I chose to put about 40% of my public portfolio in individual stocks, instead of a more conservative 20% – 30% as suggested in my article, the Recommended Split Between Passive And Active Investing. I broke my own rule.

Jensen made the mess. I decided how much it could cost me.

I also never priced in key man risk. Jensen ran Nvidia for 33 years and the company had no successor ready. When one person is the company, his personal life is part of your investment. I need to bake that into my model.

Sources indicate that and here’s the kicker. Going passive wouldn’t have 100% saved me. Nvidia is one of the largest holdings in both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. My index funds got dinged too. Passive investing doesn’t remove the Jensen risk. It only dilutes it.

Recent findings suggest that since the Fed started aggressively hiking rates in 2022, real estate has gotten little love. Mortgage rates follow the 10-year Treasury yield, which shot up, and demand softened across the country. Meanwhile, the S&P 500, especially tech and AI stocks, grabbed the spotlight.

This Nvidia debacle reminded me why I prefer owning real estate over stocks. Living in your primary residence and having it appreciate it the background is easy.

Sources indicate that as a landlord, I have a high internal locus of control. I choose the tenants. I decide when to fix the roof, remodel the kitchen or replace the carpet. I set rents within the law. If the property underperforms, it’s usually on me.

And because I can make it better, I feel more confident and happier owning it.

No CEO can tank the value of my house with a bad decision in his personal life.

Real estate still has risks. Insurance covers the physical ones like fire and water damage, and with separate policies, earthquakes and floods. But insurance won’t protect you from a local recession, a spike in mortgage rates or a shift in rent laws.

Your property can absolutely lose value. It just won’t drop 20% in a week because one person made a bad decision.

Sure, real estate may only appreciate 3% to 5% a year compared to roughly 10% for the S&P 500. But with 20% down, 4% appreciation is a 20% return on your equity before costs.

Plus you collect rent every month, and that rent doesn’t shrink the property’s value the way a dividend shrinks a firm’s cash pile. In this regard, rental income is superior to dividend income.

Industry observers note that the older I get, the more I value steady over spectacular. I’d rather not watch $20,000 vanish in a few days.

In a recent development, here’s the funny thing. Say it turned out I was the International Personal Finance Playboy of the World, with multiple girlfriends and a dozen kids like Elon Musk. As an Asian American, I'd be crucified and it would be a scandal in the personal finance community.

Recent findings suggest that if Financial Samurai were a publicly traded penny stock, the shares might drop. Then again, bad PR is still PR. Some media outlets might cover it, traffic would surge and the stock would probably go up.

But my real estate wouldn’t care either way. However bad a husband or father I might be, my properties won’t lose value because of my behavior. As an an investor, that's a beautiful thing.

In a recent development, the only ways my real estate goes down are if the local economy turns or I neglect the properties and stop keeping tenants happy and rents at market. Both are mostly in my control.

So real estate remains my favorite asset class for building wealth. It provides necessary shelter and generates a lot more income than dividends to help you break free from work sooner.

For the playboys and playgirls out there, it might be even more valuable.

According to recent reports, now for the contradiction. The older and wealthier I get, the less I want to be the landlord dealing with leaky toilets and tenant turnovers. I’ve been slowly selling physical rentals and reinvesting in private real estate for more passive income.

Doesn’t that mean giving up control? Yes.

But I’ve realized control was never the whole point. What I really want to avoid is single-person risk. A diversified pool of rental homes can't be taken down by a single person. One bad tenant or one bad house doesn’t sink it. You still have to trust the fund manager, so do your homework there too.

Sources indicate that the healthiest locus of control is neither fully internal nor fully external. Control what you can: your savings rate, your asset allocation, your position sizes and the properties you choose to own. Then accept what you can’t, without feeling helpless.

Peter Gray’s point is that kids build an internal locus of control by doing hard things on their own: playing, exploring, failing and figuring it out without an adult hovering.

Industry observers note that investing works the same way. You build confidence by making decisions, owning the results and adjusting. Losing $50,000 in Nvidia this quickly stings. But if it forces me to size positions better, it’ll make me a better investor over time.

It has been revealed that kids learn the same lesson in a different way. That’s one reason I want mine helping with tenant turnovers and rental property maintenance. Patching a wall, helping me do landscaping projects, and seeing a rental get leased teaches them that their effort changes outcomes.

According to recent reports, sometimes it’s nice to outsource your financial and parenting duties to competent people. Just make sure they’re actually competent.

The last thing you want is to pay someone for worse results than you could have gotten yourself.

Industry observers note that how much of your portfolio is in individual stocks, and have you ever lost massive because of one executive’s behavior? Does owning real estate make you feel more in control, or more stressed? Do you factor key man risk into founder-led companies? And for the parents out there, are you giving your kids enough room to develop an internal locus of control?

According to recent reports, AI may be the next general-purpose technology, but compute needs physical buildings and power. One way to get exposure without owning a single chip stock is through private real estate and venture.

Recent findings suggest that check out Fundrise, which invests in residential and industrial real estate and private AI companies. No CEO scandal can sink a diversified portfolio of properties. Fundrise is a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai.

Walking and Canoeing from Kansas to the Gulf of Mexico

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from New Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States.
  • It has been revealed that robert Cowden and Enzo.
  • When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from New Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

It has been revealed that robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition.

When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

It has been revealed that during the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

Recent findings suggest that “The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden shows the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition.

Sources indicate that cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They rolled out the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

In a recent development, it’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re currently on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.

U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).
  • According to recent reports, the team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style.
  • On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

According to recent reports, the team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell.

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

The expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

Industry observers note that after the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram.

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell mentioned. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

Sources indicate that the line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

In a recent development, on the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:.

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It has been revealed that it took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

Industry observers note that the three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

According to recent reports, the hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

Industry observers note that “You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”.

Sources indicate that he added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”.

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell said. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

It has been revealed that childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell mentioned.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”.

Industry observers note that “Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”.

#79557. Industry News: Deciding Between A Dream House And Millions In Anthropic Stock

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2516 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Deciding Between A Dream House And Millions In Anthropic Stock

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that with Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before.
  • In a recent development, so let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco.
  • Sources indicate that option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before. Further, they're experiencing FOMO or regret in not investing more in Anthropic earlier.

In a recent development, so let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco. You get to pick one, and only one:.

Sources indicate that option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco. Free and clear. Move in tomorrow.

Option 2: $8.5 million of Anthropic stock at whatever it prices at, with a six-month lockup.

My first goal is to set the line like a bookie would, splitting readers as close to 50/50 as I can.

My second goal is to get you thinking about what the money is actually for. Follow the chain backwards. You take the job for the equity and hope there's huge upside. You want the windfall to buy a house. And you want the house because that’s where your family lives.

Option 1 hands you the end of that chain today. No lockup, no tax bill, no waiting. That is the whole debate.

Sources indicate that you probably noticed Option 2 is worth more on paper. That is not a thumb on the scale. It is the tax code.

Industry observers note that A house and a share of stock are not the same currency. One is an after-tax asset that throws off shelter every single day. The other is a pre-tax asset that throws off nothing at all.

In a recent development, to convert Anthropic stock into a $7.5 million house in California, you need $11.92 million of stock at long-term capital gains rates. That is 20% federal, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, plus 13.3% to California. A 37.1% haircut.

And that is the friendly version. If your shares are RSUs that vest at the IPO, they get taxed as ordinary income. Now you need $15.84 million of stock to buy the same house.

In a recent development, quick note for early employees: qualified small business stock could wipe out a chunk of that federal bill. But Anthropic blew past the $50 million gross assets test years ago, so this only helps a very small number of people who got shares in 2021.

According to recent reports, so a $7.5 million house is worth roughly $11.9 million of Anthropic stock today. I set the line at $8.5 million because the stock also gets four years to grow, and the house does not grow nearly as fast.

According to recent reports, I have a long-standing belief that equity in a firm is a type of funny money. The value is based on growth and profit assumptions years into the future. A stock provides no utility. Its value can tank overnight, like we've seen with NVIDIA and many tech stocks recently. You can look at it on a screen, but that's about it.

In a recent development, only when you sell it and buy something does it become real. And the moment you sell it, the government takes a third or more.

A house is different. A house pays you every single day in the form of shelter you do not have to rent. Your goal in getting rich from stock is to buy the dream house, not the other way around.

In a recent development, owning that $7.5 million home outright costs $117,750 a year, and property taxes are almost the whole story at $87,750. Utilities, gardening, and services run $15,000. Maintenance on a freshly remodeled house is about $10,000. Insurance is $5,000. So “free and clear” still costs you $9,812 a month before you buy a single grocery.

But renting the same house in San Francisco costs about $25,000 a month, a 4% gross yield. So owning it beats renting it by $182,250 a year, and that gap grows. Over the six-month lockup alone, that is $91,125 handed to a landlord while you wait for permission to sell.

Proposition 13. Your assessment is locked at your purchase price and can only rise 2% a year. If the house doubles, your tax bill does not. Meanwhile your stock's tax bill grows right alongside the gain.

The $500,000 exclusion. A married couple shields half a million of gain when they sell a primary residence. Anthropic stock gets zero exclusion.

You can borrow against it without triggering a taxable event. Try getting a line of credit against locked-up pre-IPO shares.

And there is the part that does not show up in a spreadsheet. Your kids get bedrooms. You might get a rare enclosed front yard, or the sunset ocean view at 7pm. You cannot raise a family inside a brokerage account.

Now let me argue against myself, because the bull case is not stupid.

Anthropic's 2026 annualized revenue run rate is about $80 billion, up from roughly $47 billion in May and about $9 billion at the end of 2025. The firm also reported its first positive adjusted operating income, reversing a loss of about $5.6 billion in 2024.

Industry observers note that here is my pro forma, and I am deliberately staying inside the tech giant's own guidance. I have the run rate at $90 billion by December 2026, $150 billion by December 2027, and $200 billion by December 2028. Growth decelerates from 67% to 33%, which is still extraordinary for a business of that size.

Sources indicate that if those numbers land, which I think they will because companies sandbag their first guidance, the multiple does the work for you. Whatever Anthropic prices at, that number gets cut roughly in half by the end of 2027 and in half again by the end of 2028. The tech giant simply grows into the price.

Sources indicate that A house is not going to do that. A house is going to sit there and appreciate at optimistically 10% per annum, but probably closer to 5%, while asking you for a latest roof.

Say you take the $8.5 million in Anthropic stock, ride out the lockup, and initiative to buy your dream house with an enclosed front yard in four years.

Recent findings suggest that the house is not waiting for you. At 5% appreciation, $7.5 million becomes $9.1 million. And while you wait, you are renting at $25,000 a month, which burns about $1.27 million over four years.

So the stock has to produce $10.4 million after tax just to get you back to even. Pre-tax, that means your $8.5 million stock has to become $16.5 million. The extra $6.1 million goes to the government.

Sources indicate that anthropic has to appreciate 1.9 times, from wherever it prices, within four years. Call it a double. That is an 18.1% compound annual return.

If it prices at $1.4 trillion, you need $2.7 trillion. If it prices at $1.5 trillion, you need $2.9 trillion. The dollar figure moves. The requirement does not. The house costs what it costs, rent costs what it costs, and California takes what it takes. None of that cares what Goldman and Morgan Stanley settle on tonight.

Recent findings suggest that A 50% gain is not enough. Up 50% leaves you with $8 million after tax, more than a million short of the asking price alone, and $2.4 million short once you count the rent you burned getting there.

If growth keeps decelerating, from 33% in 2028 to 25% in 2029 to 20% in 2030, the run rate reaches roughly $300 billion by the time the four years are up.

So the real question is what multiple of that $300 billion the market has to pay for you to break even.

Recent findings suggest that mature software companies trade at 6 to 10 times sales. Run the math across the range and there is a clean dividing line at about $1.54 trillion.

Price below that, and break-even only requires an ordinary multiple. At $1.4 trillion you need the market to pay 9.1 times sales in 2030. At $1.5 trillion, 9.7 times. Both sit inside the normal band. The stock wins even if Anthropic gets re-rated down to a perfectly boring software manufacturer.

It has been revealed that price above $1.54 trillion, and break-even requires a premium multiple that still has to be there four years from now. That is a different bet entirely, because it depends on sentiment rather than execution.

For perspective, back in September, when Anthropic was floating a $2 trillion valuation, break-even required 13 times sales.

SpaceX went public in June at around $1.75 trillion. It surged past $2 trillion, then fell back. It has been a volatile stock out of the gate, and Anthropic may trade the same way.

That is the thing about a six-month lockup. You do not get to sell into the euphoria. You get to watch it, and then you get to find out what is left when everybody else's lockup expires on the same day as yours.

The other half of this trade is that San Francisco real estate is in a melt-up, driven by the exact wealth we are discussing.

Between January and late June 2026, 136 single-family homes closed at or above $5 million, more than double the 67 transactions in the same period a year earlier. In June alone, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million over asking. At the very top, even all-cash offers of $25 million and up have been outbid.

This remodeled Victorian on Castro St. sold in September for $7,650,000 against a $5,495,000 list. That is 39% over asking, $2.15 million above what the sellers hoped for, for 3,416 square feet on a 2,622 square foot lot. Smaller than the house in our scenario. This is what the money actually buys here.

A 4,500 square foot remodeled home on a large lot with views is a unicorn property. Homes with views usually don’t have large useable lots and vice versa. Maybe 5-8 trade in a given year. If you wait four years to buy it with your stock proceeds, you are not bidding against today's buyers. You are bidding against every other newly liquid Anthropic and OpenAI employee who made the same initiative you did.

Instead of the $7.5 million house being worth $9.1 million in four years, it could be worth well north of $10 million.

Sources indicate that that is the trap. Everybody's exit strategy is the same few houses.

Some of you are already typing that the answer is to take the stock and move somewhere a mansion costs $2 million. Two problems.

The job that created the windfall is in San Francisco, so leaving means leaving the equity behind. And California taxes equity compensation based on where you worked while it vested, so moving after the fact does not get you out of the bill you are trying to avoid.

Further, would you really walk away from a job like that when there are so many more millions to make? Only if you’re a FIRE person who values time and freedom more than money.

It has been revealed that as for the mansion itself, I toured a bunch of them in Honolulu last summer and came away thinking buying a mansion in paradise might be backwards. Then again, having a mansion in a beautiful city like San Francisco is a pretty amazing combination.

Real wealth is not the number. Real wealth is the gap between what you own and what you can actually enjoy.

It has been revealed that you can spend the next four years watching a ticker and eating at home to preserve optionality, and end up with $10.4 million and four years of your kids' childhoods spent in a sub-optional rental you did not love. Or you can spend those four years in the dream house, providing for your family and making memories, and end up with $9.1 million or more of home equity plus four years you actually lived.

Recent findings suggest that that remarked, I believe Anthropic could reach $3 trillion in market cap by the end of 2027 and $5 trillion by the end of 2028. Against anything in tonight's IPO price range, that is a healthy amount of upside. If I am right, the stock wins this debate within about thirteen months and it is not even a contest.

Recent findings suggest that I drew the fair line myself, and I am still leaning toward the house. Watching names like Google and Nvidia drop 30% to 40% in a few months is a reminder of how fickle stocks are. And not having to fight a bidding war over a unicorn property would save my wife and me a lot of heartbreak.

At 49 with two young kids, time is too precious to put my life on hold for money that won't be used. I might end up with far more money holding Anthropic stock. But by the time I sell and pay the capital gains, I doubt I can lock down the dream house at a reasonable price.

Because if I have $20 million in Anthropic stock in four years, so do thousands of other employees and investors. Bidding against one buyer is hard enough. Bidding against dozens for the same unicorn property is impossible to win. And what good is money you cannot convert into the thing you wanted it for?

So I take the bird in hand. I have watched enough people optimize their way through a decade and arrive at the finish line wealthy and vaguely disappointed. Money is a means to an end. And one of those ends is living in the nicest house you can comfortably afford.

Recent findings suggest that readers, Which would you take: the $7.5 million dream house, or $8.5 million of Anthropic stock with a six-month lockup? And why? Note: All your comments eventually go through. The spam filter is just working overdrive. Thanks for your patience.

Industry observers note that most people reading this will not be deciding between a $7.5 million house and an IPO windfall. But the same AI boom driving both is also driving something more boring: the physical buildout underneath it. Every model needs compute, compute needs data centers, and data centers need land, power, and permits. That is real estate, and it is the constraint nobody can code their way around.

Sources indicate that fundrise lets you invest in real estate with a low minimum, including the industrial and residential assets sitting in the path of that buildout. I’ve been an investor since 2016. Fundrise is a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai.

Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S.
  • Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails.
  • Before starting the journey on September 17, he remarked they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he remarked they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

Industry observers note that they started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

According to recent reports, the route. Photo: Pete Streufert.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to Upcoming Mexico.

Industry observers note that paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert.

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

It has been revealed that the pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram.

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu.
  • In a recent development, joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass.
  • Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

In a recent development, joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

Sources indicate that in practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to problem its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Sources indicate that cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#79550. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (619 w)

West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time.
  • Sources indicate that andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening.
  • “So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Sources indicate that andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”.

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev.

Recent findings suggest that first, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev remarked. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”.

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Sources indicate that on their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” mentioned Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:.

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Sources indicate that rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

Industry observers note that the route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

According to recent reports, the only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

In a recent development, objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he remarked.

#79547. Breaking: The Honor Tax: Refusing To Play The Game Will Cost You

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2170 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Honor Tax: Refusing To Play The Game Will Cost You

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.
  • According to recent reports, I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares.
  • But naively, I indicated a true order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.

According to recent reports, I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares. That’s 4.6% of my indication, or about $5,000 out of $107,900. I entered my order the morning the books opened, hoping that would signal I was a serious buyer.

But naively, I indicated a true order. I wanted up to $107,900 of stock to reach my goal of roughly $500,000 in Anthropic exposure through traditional VC, public VC, and direct ownership.

The embarrassing part is that I should have known better. During my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse, I worked on over 100 IPOs. I went on roadshows, introduced management to my institutional clients, and read demand back to the syndicate desk. Everybody padded their orders. A fund that wanted 500,000 shares would put in for 2 million because it knew the syndicate desk would cut it back.

It has been revealed that the problem with being honorable is that you lose when everybody else is inflating their order to get their true allocation. I thought being a Fidelity customer for over 25 years, with my kids’ 529 plans, custodial accounts, Roth IRAs, a SEP IRA, and Solo 401(k)s, would count for something. It clearly didn’t. To them, I’m just a number, like most people who work are.

The allocation process reminded me that if you want to compete in this hyper-competitive world, you have to work the system to your advantage. If you don’t, you will likely lose to those who do.

To protest my insultingly low allocation, I decided to take the day off. But that’s what I do every day anyway.

Here are some real-life examples where playing fair cost money, time, and happiness.

When my wife and I applied to preschools for our son, we decided not to ask our network to write letters of recommendation to the school heads. Despite having friends who were substantial donors and board members, I wanted to see if we could get in on our own merits as a high school tennis coach and his editor wife.

Sources indicate that we could not. Six preschools rejected us after happily taking our $75 to $100 application fees. We only got into our neighborhood preschool through serendipity. We kept running into one of their teachers on paternity leave in Golden Gate Park.

If we had leaned on our connections, we would have saved hundreds in application fees, dozens of hours, and a lot of stress.

Recent findings suggest that the families who got in weren’t less honorable. They were more effective. Our honor tax came to six rejection letters and several hundred dollars in application fees.

I first thought about starting Financial Samurai in 2006, the year I graduated from Cal’s MBA program. But I didn’t because I felt I needed at least 10 years of finance experience before I had the credibility to write publicly.

Sources indicate that so I waited until the world was falling apart in 2009, 10 years after graduating from William & Mary. The three-year delay cost me revenue, likely earlier book deals, a bigger reputation, and probably pushed back my exit from finance by at least a year. I wrote more about this in Don’t Let Honor And Pride Keep You On Hard Mode Forever.

The internet has shown me time and again that you do NOT need expertise in what you’re talking about or selling. A not-rich 26-year-old can write a book on how to get rich. Someone whose marriage is falling apart and doesn't have kids can host a podcast for couples with kids. Someone with a $100,000 portfolio can become an investing guru on social media.

Plenty of people overlook your experience or credentials. So you might as well put yourself out there and start.

In a recent development, after 13 years of grade school and four years of college, you might have too much pride to accept money from your parents. Making it on your own feels like the honorable thing to do. It’s also good for your self-esteem.

According to recent reports, so you sleep on a friend’s couch and lose weight because you can barely afford groceries. Meanwhile, your college friends rent nice two-bedrooms in the city and go out every weekend because their parents are paying. Some even buy their first homes and have their girlfriends move in, courtesy of the Bank of Mom and Dad.

You, on the other hand, turn down an amazing job offer in Newly introduced York City because it’s way too expensive. Instead, you stay in Des Moines, Iowa, take a $60,000 job with benefits, and feel like you’ve made it.

At your 10-year college reunion, you’ve finally saved $100,000 and are ready to settle down. But the girl you liked moved to NYC to be with your college buddy, who is now a director at a hedge fund making $1 million a year.

He’s worth $7 million and no longer needs his parents’ help. So he buys a $6 million, three-bedroom condo on the Upper West Side, marries your dream girl, and starts a family.

Industry observers note that his parents’ help wasn’t a handout. It was a launch pad. Your pride was an anchor. More parents would rather help their adult children while still alive than after they are gone. Accept help with grace.

Industry observers note that in 2012, I wanted out of banking. The classic move would have been to give two weeks’ notice, thank everyone, and walk away. That’s what most people do, leaving their deferred compensation and any chance of severance on the table.

Instead, I negotiated. I offered to train my junior colleague to take over my business, which gave management a smooth transition. In exchange, I kept five years of deferred compensation and walked away with a six-figure severance check. That money gave me a multi-year runway to grow Financial Samurai and remain free.

Had I just quit, my honor tax would have been five years of deferred compensation plus a six-figure severance check. That’s an expensive way to feel good about yourself, when companies treat you as a number and rapidly move on once you’re gone.

I break down the exact process in How To Engineer Your Layoff if you're looking to leave with a severance package as well.

You’d have to be naive to think a wealthy parent who virtue signals about how amazing public schools are, but sends their own kids to private school, would ever give up their kid’s college spot for yours.

It has been revealed that the world is extremely cutthroat. Yes, you will have good friends and good people who try to help you. But in most competitive situations, you’re up against people who care about themselves and their families first.

It has been revealed that in my IPO example, my competitors were the thousands of other retail investors who wanted shares. If I had inflated my order by 10X, I might have gotten about $50,000 of stock instead of $5,000. With a 15% first-day pop, that’s a $7,500 gain instead of $750.

So whatever credentials or goodwill you have, don’t assume they mean much. At every competitive juncture, you must speak up and market yourself. People will forget who you are and what you’ve done for them if you don’t remind them.

In a recent development, working the system doesn’t mean lying, cheating, or stepping on people. It means understanding how the game is actually scored so you stop paying an honor tax you don’t owe. Here’s how.

Industry observers note that 1) Inventory your unfair advantages. Write down your network, capital, credentials, platform, free time, and family support. Most people underestimate what they have because they’ve never made the list.

2) Learn how the game is really scored. IPO books get padded. Admissions offices respond to relationships and donations. Many jobs get filled through referrals before they’re ever posted. Find an insider and ask how decisions actually get made. The official rules are often only half the story.

According to recent reports, 3) Make the ask early. A referral, an introduction, or a note from a board member costs your friend five minutes. Getting rejected six times costs you far more. Most people are happy to help. They just need to be asked.

In a recent development, 4) Negotiate everything with leverage. A competing job offer, a severance package, a retention offer from your cable tech giant, a lower rate from your lender. If you don’t ask, the answer is always no.

5) Accept help with gratitude, then pay it forward. Taking help from parents, mentors, or friends isn’t weakness. It’s compounding. The honorable part is what you do with the head start.

According to recent reports, 6) Remind people of your value. Send the patch email. Check in with the fund manager. Tell your longtime broker you’d like a bigger allocation next time. Silence gets read as indifference.

7) Know your line and your risk. Padding an IPO order is common, but there’s a catch. If demand comes in weaker than expected, you could get filled on everything you asked for. Never inflate an order you can’t afford to pay for. Game the system, but don’t break the law or your word.

Be honorable with your family, your friends, and anyone who trusts you. Keep your word. Pay your debts.

Sources indicate that but when you’re competing for a scarce resource against strangers, following an honor code nobody else follows isn’t noble. It’s expensive. And the cost compounds over decades in the form of lost money, lost time, and lost happiness.

Industry observers note that if you’re a parent, it’s your responsibility to fight to give your children every chance to survive and thrive. Your kids won’t care that you were too proud to make a phone call. They’ll care whether they got the opportunity.

Industry observers note that as I wrap up this post, I have a confession. Maybe honor wasn’t the only reason I placed a true order.

Recent findings suggest that between my traditional venture funds and public venture funds, I already own a meaningful amount of Anthropic. So deep down, I probably felt my exposure was big enough. If I had really needed those shares, I suspect I would have padded my order like everybody else.

It has been revealed that in other words, maybe I just didn’t care that much if my order got cut by 95%. I’m at a stage in life where I should have enough. Missing out on a $7,500 first-day pop won’t change how I live, where my kids go to school, or what time I wake up tomorrow.

According to recent reports, which makes me wonder whether our actions show our real financial position better than our words do. The person who fights hardest for every share, every school spot, and every introduction is often the person who feels they don’t have enough yet. They say they are financially independent, yet stay for one more year at a job they hate. The person who shrugs may simply be full.

So before you judge yourself for being too honorable, or someone else for working the system, ask what each of you actually needs.

Sometimes the honor tax is a choice. Sometimes it’s just a sign you can afford to pay it.

According to recent reports, have you ever lost out because you played by the rules while others didn’t? Did you pad your order in the Anthropic IPO, and how much did you get relative to your true demand? Where do you draw the line between leveraging your advantages and gaming the system unfairly?

Sources indicate that would you accept financial help from your parents to get ahead, or is making it on your own still worth the price? And if you have kids, how hard are you willing to work your network to give them a better shot?

Do you think your willingness to play hardball shrinks once you feel you have enough?

Most people don’t fall behind financially because they’re lazy. They fall behind because they play by rules nobody else follows. They accept the first offer, wait their turn, and hope someone notices.

In Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller, I show you how to build wealth on purpose. It covers the right net worth targets for your age, how to multiply your income, and how to use every advantage you have to reach seven figures and beyond.

Building wealth also means getting the major decisions right. Buy This Not That, a WSJ bestseller, is my framework for life’s most expensive choices: how much house to buy, how to invest, how to negotiate, and when to take a risk. One good decision can easily make up for years of honor tax.

  • It has been revealed that since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks.
  • The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr.
  • The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World.

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

In a recent development, “I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”.

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more notable to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Photo: Ole Bielfeldt/Nikon Small World.

Industry observers note that ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World.

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World.

It has been revealed that in defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

In a recent development, these human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World.

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

According to recent reports, you can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum.

According to recent reports, you can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously.
  • But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear.
  • The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

It has been revealed that they left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families noted they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

It has been revealed that kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

According to recent reports, “Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Recent findings suggest that multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities confirmed they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

  • In a recent development, the incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday.
  • Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

In a recent development, the incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok remarked that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

According to recent reports, eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Recent findings suggest that turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

In a recent development, turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Industry observers note that jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet.

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.
  • ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months.
  • Recent findings suggest that views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Recent findings suggest that views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

According to recent reports, piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot complications in today’s mountaineering.

It has been revealed that simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides.

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

It has been revealed that the members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

It has been revealed that that led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Major List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively newly introduced piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas mentioned the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Industry observers note that interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the massive list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

Recent findings suggest that as for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

In a recent development, buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Recent findings suggest that the physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

Industry observers note that next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.
