📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

According to recent reports, the storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

Sources indicate that driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

In a recent development, with hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better firm but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

In Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

Gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

The reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the upcoming windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

It’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

‘Over the Moon.’ Ohio Hunter Shoots 215-Inch Buck from Her Favorite Stand on Her Birthday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that southeastern Ohio is known for its heavily wooded rolling hills and the big bucks that live there.
  • Sources indicate that the substantial deer started showing up on trail camera about a month ago, although only at night.
  • According to recent reports, “It was bitter cold that day, but I hunted from the morning until noon,” Fuller tells Outdoor Life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that southeastern Ohio is known for its heavily wooded rolling hills and the big bucks that live there. Margaret Fuller of New Plymouth has hunted a small piece of private land there for years, and it’s where she was hunting this past weekend. In particular, she was looking for a giant 200-class buck she’d come to think of as “the Monarch.”.

Sources indicate that the substantial deer started showing up on trail camera about a month ago, although only at night. He was hitting scrapes near one of Fuller’s favorite ladder stands, and that’s where she hunted on Friday.

According to recent reports, “It was bitter cold that day, but I hunted from the morning until noon,” Fuller tells Outdoor Life. “I went inside to get warm for a while, then went back out that afternoon and hunted until dark.”.

That day she spotted a smaller buck about 50 yards from her stand. The deer was working along a trail toward her, but seemed to sense something was wrong and slipped away.

Fuller returned to that same stand the next day — her birthday — anyway. It’s the same spot she killed a 178-inch buck in 2022 during the firearms season.

“I didn’t get on stand until about noon,” notes Fuller, a financial program manager for the Ohio Department of Natural Resources, “because I was so cold from the previous day’s hunt.”.

It has been revealed that about 3 p.m. she heard an ATV roaring on the neighbor’s property and she thought her hunt that afternoon was over.

According to recent reports, “But a few minutes later I heard something in the woods, and then I caught a little movement,” says Fuller. “I stood up, grabbed my crossbow, and saw it was Monarch.”.

He was at 50 yards and coming to a scrape along the same trail the little buck had walked the day before.

“I was worried the Monarch would spook, too, like the smaller buck did. I knew I had to shoot soon before he caught my wind.”.

The buck began stopped to rub his rack on a tree, then started walking closer to Fuller.

“I knew I had to stop him before he got to the place where he could smell me, so I grunted,” claims Fuller. “He stopped when I grunted, and I shot him at 30 yards.”.

Instead of running, the buck dropped right there. Her shot had struck the spine, and the deer didn’t get up.

Fuller called her sons and husband, then climbed down from her ladder stand.

In a recent development, “I was on cloud nine,” she claims. “I’ve been hunting deer since I was 14 with my dad, and I’d have given anything for him to have been with me and see this buck … And it was on my birthday, too!”.

The family helped Fuller snap photos and field-dress the massive nontypical, which had 20 points. Then they butchered the deer at home.

The whitetail, which Fuller estimates is 5½ years old, was scored at 213 inches by Buckmasters measurer Toby Hughes.

“I’m over the moon,” notes Fuller, who credits her success, in part, to “sticking with hunting even in the coldest weather.”.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

She also adds that practicing meticulous scent control with her clothing and using a cover scent probably didn’t hurt, either.

Sources indicate that “But the best thing is the joy of having my sons and husband involved in hunting. Everyone helped me and that family camaraderie is really special.”.

10 of the Hottest Hunting Suppressors on the Market in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • It has been revealed that it’s never been easier to get a suppressor for your hunting rifle.
  • I’ve been shooting every latest suppressor I can get my hands on for years, and these are the best ones that I have used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

It has been revealed that it’s never been easier to get a suppressor for your hunting rifle. But choosing one, for a first-time buyer, can be intimidating. There are thousands of options on the market and narrowing it down to the best can for your hunting rifle isn’t easy if you don’t know what to look for. So many new suppressors are hitting the market that what was a top-of-the-line can a couple years ago is just average today.

I’ve been shooting every latest suppressor I can get my hands on for years, and these are the best ones that I have used.

It has been revealed that this is one of the best hunting rifle suppressors I have ever used. Like many others that are leading the pack, it’s 3D printed from titanium, making it both strong and economical. It measures 5 inches long and weighs just 5.75 ounces. Despite its lightweight profile, it’s very quiet. In fact, it’s substantially quieter than several other popular suppressors — something I noted on a recent antelope hunt.

This is one of my top picks because it’s simple, rugged, quiet, and you’ll hardly notice it on your muzzle. It is direct thread only and, because threads are cut into the suppressor itself, they cannot be changed like a HUB-compatible suppressor. For a hunting suppressor, that’s a feature, not a bug. At $900, this is a really good value. Many top-level hunting suppressors will cost you $1,000 or more.

In the year since its introduction, Airlock has released 30-cal and 7mm versions of the Zero Gravity, as well as a 3.7-ounce Zero Gravity Nano, which is designed for bolt-action centerfire .22 cals like the 22 ARC, 22 Creed, and .22-250 Rem. It’s slightly larger than a rimfire suppressor, but satisfyingly quiet.

The Nomad Ti XC is another excellent option for a hunting suppressor. Its 3D printed design allows for modern baffles and reduces weak spots. The front and rear of the can are threaded and it is compatible with HUB rear mounts. I prefer using a Silencerco Ti direct thread adapter on the rear, and the standard .308 front cap. Other companies like Salmon River Solutions are making accessories like a directional brake that threads into the front cap to further reduce recoil and tame down cartridges like the .300 PRC. As pictured, the suppressor weighs less than 10 ounces and works wonderfully for anything 30-caliber and under. A nice feature is the inclusion of deep tool notches which makes removing the HUB mounts easy without worry of damaging the suppressor.

Recent findings suggest that another great option, if you want a shorter overall length for your rifle, is the Nomad TiOTB, which has a chamber that extends back over the barrel. This suppressor has the same interchangeable endcaps, but works exclusively with a thread-over-brake mount.

In a recent development, I’ve been shooting the TiTrex 300 Ti for several months now, and this is one of the best options for a general-purpose hunting suppressor out there. After all that shooting, it still only weighs 9.5 ounces, and it offers great mounting and front-cap modularity.

It has been revealed that A couple years ago, the Silencerco Scythe Ti was one of few .30-cal silencers that light, but it’s been plagued by weld failure problems. The TiTrex 300 Ti is also made of titanium, is slightly lighter, and uses HUB mounts at the rear and an open-source front cap that works with the Silencerco Bravo front mounts. You can use a normal endcap or the short endcap brake, which helps reduce recoil, and both have great spanner wrench notches. It’s also compatible with some aftermarket Endcap brakes like the Salmon River Solutions Grim, which can help cut recoil even more.

The TiTrex has a 3D-printed body and baffle system that is rugged, durable, and even full-auto rated. This is a great option to use with a front brake as a competition can, but that can also work well on your hunting rifle. It would also be a solid choice as your first suppressor. A unique feature is that the serialized portion of the suppressor is a stainless-steel band at the rear of the can, that can be moved to a different core if you manage to wear the original out or damage it somehow.

According to recent reports, there are three big trends in hunting suppressors in 2026, and the Buckskin 30 from Tenet tackles all of them. First, it’s 3D printed. Additive manufacturing has allowed companies to quickly develop and prototype suppressor models while reducing weak points like welds on thin titanium.

Sources indicate that second, it incorporates a front brake. Suppressors reduce recoil by slowing gases as they exit the muzzle, and incorporating a brake on the front tames them even further. The Buckskin features a built-in brake that is non-adjustable and won’t come loose.

It has been revealed that third, it’s light. It’s printed with titanium and mine weighs 8.5 ounces — making it the lightest .30-cal suppressor I own. I’ve used this suppressor on my 20-inch 300 PRC, several 6.5 Creedmoors, and have been putting a lot of rounds through it on a 16-inch 7mm Backcountry. It does a great job at reducing recoil while adding minimal extra weight.

Industry observers note that if you want more adjustability and increased recoil reduction, the Tenet Limited 30 is another suppressor to look at. These are more expensive, but feature a removable front brake that cuts your rifle movement dramatically. Mine has a two-port brake and, while the first generation of brakes tended to blast your face with gas, the recently-released gen 2 brake has small steps in the curved brake to disrupt that gas impulse. It’s much more pleasant. If spotting your impacts with larger cartridges is important to you, a can like this fits the bill.

In the days of year-long waiting periods, modularity was king for hunting suppressors. While modular cans have their place, a simple dedicated hunting silencer is hard to beat. This fully 3D-printed titanium can from Unknown Munitions weighs about 11 ounces and features a reflex design, meaning the rear portion of the suppressor goes back over the barrel. That reflex expansion chamber allows a shorter portion — about four inches — to stick out in front of your muzzle. This improves balance and gives you a more compact package than the average 8-inch suppressor. The reflex design also creates a noticeably duller sound signature, whereas some produce a very sharp, snappy sound.

These are available in .30 caliber as well as 6.5mm and 6mm options, and models and fit over 0.75-inch diameter steel barrels and the OGL model fits larger carbon-fiber barrels. This suppressor isn’t modular, so you need to ensure compatibility before you order. Also check out their Reaper suppressor, which I haven’t had the chance to use, but should be another top contender.

Sources indicate that I’ve used several of B&T’s Print-X series of titanium 3D-printed suppressors and have been impressed by all of them. Their modular VERS36 Ti model, however, deserves special recognition. To my knowledge, this is the lightest modular 36-caliber suppressor on the market, and it’s way cheaper than similar, more primitive cans were several years ago. If you’re wanting to get a suppressor to start out with, or to use on multiple hunting rifles, this is your jam.

Sources indicate that it’s got 36-caliber baffles and comes with a .360 front cap. The rear is HUB-compatible and B&T makes nice titanium direct-thread adapters. You can get smaller front caps as well. If using on smaller cartridges or you just need a shorter overall package, the front section is removable. This is a flow-through design with spiral baffles that works well on bolt actions and gas-guns alike. It’s ideal for cartridges like the .350 Legend, but will work on anything with a .360-diameter bullet or smaller. I received mine through Silencer Central and it can be delivered to your door.

According to recent reports, the StingerWorx Evo Hunter is a lightweight suppressor that’s more affordable than the 3D printed titanium cans, and it’s also much more serviceable. A downside of most printed suppressors is that there isn’t a great way to remove large amounts of carbon buildup from the baffles. Soaking and ultrasonic cleaners help, but a lot of shooters want a suppressor that can be disassembled and manually cleaned.

The Evo Hunter is just over 10 ounces, and it gets there by using multiple materials. It has a titanium blast baffle and chamber to provide a long service life, but uses an aluminum baffle stack downstream of that — where heat and abrasion isn’t as intense. If damaged, that front baffle stack is replaceable. Additionally, the Evo Hunter is compatible with StingerWorx’s front brake if you’re looking for additional recoil reduction. It’s got HUB threads at the rear and the blast chamber is deep enough to work with a variety of over-brake HUB mounts that you might already have. For the light weight, versatility, and serviceability, this can is a great value.

There are lots of suppressors out there and, because many of them are so similar, lots of good ones can get lost in the mix. Because we cover a lot of leading-edge ultralight cans, don’t think that we don’t pay attention to budget options, too. There are bottom-tier suppressors that are very cheap — often made of mostly aluminum — that will work, but can also leave buyers dissatisfied. When it comes to bang for your buck, stainless steel is still one of the best materials for a more affordable can. The first suppressor I ever bought was a large .30-cal stainless can. It was durable and affordable and its weight was the only downside.

Industry observers note that the Banish HNT 30 SS is a great example of a modern great value. It’s compact and, at 13.8 ounces, not excessively heavy. It’s suitable for virtually any hunting rifle .30-caliber and smaller, and similar in size and form to the lightweight Banish Backcountry titanium can. It’s got hub threads at the rear and comes with a direct-thread adapter. If you’re looking to try a suppressor for hunting and want a good-quality can, this is a great place to start.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for maximum suppression of your big-bore cartridges, the Goliath Gen 2 from Liberty Suppressors is an excellent option. This beast of a silencer is 10.25 inches long by 2 inches in diameter and designed specifically for cartridges like the .458 Socom, .450 Bushmaster, and .45/70 Gov’t. While big, this can is relatively light. It’s got twice the volume of suppressors like the Silencerco Hybrid 46, but weighs only about 4 ounces more (22 ounces total). This is a perfect fit for anyone hunting with a short-barreled .458 or .450 Bushmaster, or a trapper-style .45/70.

According to recent reports, the suppressor has a titanium sleeve and titanium baffle stack that’s removable and serviceable so you can shoot cast lead bullets and clean out lead fouling — unlike sealed suppressors. I’ve had a Liberty .22 rimfire can for many years, and this is essentially a much larger version of that. I’ve been shooting it on my .45/70 and it’s working wonderfully on my .338 ARC SBR with subsonic ammo.

One of the best values in lightweight modular suppressors is the BDE from Primary Weapons Systems. I’ve been shooting the 5.56 model for the last several months, and it combines smart manufacturing with durability, value, and the kind of modularity a lot of hunters want. The BDE has hub threads at the rear, a blast chamber segment, and a 3D-printed main baffle segment. Forward of that, it has removable individual threaded baffle segments topped with an end cap.

This is a sealed suppressor, but baffles are designed to allow gasses to flow better and reduce backpressure, making a great option for both a bolt gun and AR-style semi-auto. Each segment of the can has wrench notches making disassembly easy, and you can customize to the platform you’ll be shooting. This has been living on my .223 practice bolt-action and the irregular surface contours do seem to help break up mirage. The BDE is also available in .30- and .36- caliber models, all with customizable baffle configurations.

Picking through the many different suppressor options can be daunting, and most good suppressors perform similarly. To find one that you’ll be happy with, consider details like construction and weight, but also the level of modularity you desire, or whether you’re just looking for a good value. If one of these isn’t quite what you’re looking for, I hope that seeing these options and features will help you home in on the model that you will be most satisfied with. The suppressor market is constantly evolving, and we will continue to use and test suppressors with the goal of helping you make the most informed decisions possible.
